summary: Ƙura Alert is a bilingual (Hausa/English) early-warning service for Gombe, Nigeria. It turns NASA aerosol, meteorology and rainfall data into plain-language daily advice, such as "Don't dry clothes outside today" or "Cover your goods, heavy dust expected," for traders, tailors, parents, schools and clinics. It forecasts harmattan dust risk on a four-level scale (Low to Severe) and gives rain-based flood warnings. Because warnings arrive in the user's own language on WhatsApp/SMS, not as technical charts, the people most affected by dust and flooding can act on them. An optional low-cost sensor node adds on-the-ground readings.
details: Ƙura Alert is a bilingual (Hausa and English) early-warning service for Gombe, Nigeria. It gives anyone in Gombe a daily hazard level and a short, plain-language instruction, such as "Don't dry clothes outside today" or "Cover your goods, heavy dust expected." The main users are traders, tailors, parents, schools, and clinics. WHAT IT DOES Users see a risk gauge with four levels (Low, Moderate, High, Severe), advice cards for laundry, market, school, and health, an evidence panel showing recent aerosol data, and a WhatsApp share button. Alerts come in the user's own language, so people can act on them without reading technical charts. HOW IT WORKS Dust risk is calculated as a single dust index that combines dust concentration, aerosol optical depth, wind, and dryness. The weights are 0.50 for dust, 0.25 for aerosol optical depth, 0.15 for wind, and 0.10 for dryness. They are rule-based and explainable, and we state openly that they are expert-chosen rather than fitted. The index is mapped to the four levels using percentile thresholds from NASA historical data covering about 605 days across four seasons. For flooding, accumulated rainfall is compared against fixed thresholds of 15, 30, and 50 mm to trigger Watch, Warning, and Severe alerts. Messages are generated from templates in Hausa and English. An optional low-cost Arduino UNO R4 WiFi sensor node (particulate sensor, temperature and humidity sensor, water-level sensor, rain gauge, buzzer, and display) can send local readings to the API. HAZARD DETECTION Harmattan dust is detected with the weighted dust index described above, using NASA MERRA-2 and POWER data. Flooding is detected from rainfall accumulation thresholds and, where a node is installed, a water-level reading. Poor air quality is covered by the sensor node's particulate readings combined with the dust index. Planned extensions use the same pipeline of fetching NASA grid data, computing an index, comparing it to local history, and generating a Hausa message. Drought and dry spells would be detected from consecutive days with little rain, rainfall anomalies, and soil moisture deficits (NASA POWER, GPM IMERG, SMAP). Crop stress would be detected from vegetation greenness anomalies (MODIS and VIIRS NDVI). Bushfires would be detected from active fire data (NASA FIRMS). Heat stress would be detected from temperature and humidity (NASA POWER). Adding any of these requires a new index and new message templates, not a new system. BENEFITS Fewer ruined goods and less laundry loss, better protection for children and people with respiratory problems, earlier flood preparation, and information that does not depend on English or technical literacy. VALIDATION MERRA-2 dust optical depth was compared with AERONET sun-photometer data (correlation 0.865, 30 samples, bias of +0.163 AOD). This validates the data source, not the forecast itself. LIMITATIONS The index weights are expert-chosen and not fitted. The nearest AERONET site (Ilorin) is far from Gombe. The live signal comes from near-real-time reanalysis and forecast data, while NASA historical data sets the baseline. Flood alerts depend on rainfall inputs and sensor placement. GOAL To build a reusable template for local-language hazard alerts that can be adapted to other Nigerian languages and regions. TOOLS Next.js, FastAPI (Python), SQLite, Arduino C++, Open-Meteo, NASA Earthdata (MERRA-2, POWER), NASA GIBS, and AERONET.
